History:
• Chief complaint: “Blinding” headache persisting for 3 days, began suddenly on waking.  
• Character: Diffuse but worse over right eye; rated 8/10, decreases to ~5/10 after ibuprofen.  
• Course: Constant; partial, temporary relief with ibuprofen; returns in full within hours.  
• Associated symptoms: Photophobia; intermittent “shooting lights” in vision; mild nausea (no vomiting). No numbness, weakness, speech difficulty, fever, cough, sinus pain, nasal bleed, weight loss, or constitutional symptoms.  
• Aggravating factors: Standing up quickly; rapid head movement.  
• Relieving factors: Ibuprofen (partial), rest; able to sleep through night, not awakened by pain.  
• Previous headaches: Only occasional mild pressure between eyes; never this severe or prolonged.  
• Family history: Mother has severe migraines with vomiting.  
• Social: Lives alone; non-smoker; alcohol ~3 drinks once weekly; no recreational drugs.  
• Review of systems otherwise unremarkable.

Past Medical History:
• No chronic illnesses reported.  
• Surgical/Hospitalization history: None mentioned.  
• Medications: 
  – Combined oral contraceptive pill (brand not stated), dose/route/frequency not documented, started ~1 yr ago.  
  – Ibuprofen 400 mg orally as needed (patient-supplied), partial relief.  
• Allergies: Denies drug or other allergies.

Physical Examination:
(Telemedicine visit; no in-person exam performed)  
• General: Patient appears alert, coherent speech.  
• Neurologic: No self-reported focal weakness, sensory loss, or speech disturbance.  
• Eyes: Reports photophobia and visual “shooting lights”; no documented fundoscopic exam.  
• No objective vitals, funduscopy, or neurologic exam obtained.

Impression:
Persistent 3-day moderate-to-severe headache with photophobia and visual disturbance—probable migraine vs secondary headache; requires in-person neurologic and ocular evaluation.

Management Plan:
• Medication: Will prescribe a stronger NSAID (name/dose not documented) to replace ibuprofen; may take paracetamol concurrently. Instructed to take with food.  
• Arrange face-to-face appointment with clinic support team for:  
  – Full neurologic examination.  
  – Fundoscopic (optic disc) assessment.  
  – Blood pressure measurement and contraceptive pill review.  
• Contingency: If headache worsens, changes character, or becomes unbearable before appointment, patient to attend Emergency Department (A&E) or call service for advice.  
• Education: Discussed potential link between combined OCP and migraine with aura; may require pill change after evaluation.  
• Follow-up: Appointment booking advised; cancel if symptoms fully resolve before then.

Patient Summary:
A previously healthy young woman reports her first severe, persistent 3-day global headache with photophobia and brief visual phenomena. Clinical picture suggests migraine, but duration and new onset warrant neurological and ocular examination. She was given interim analgesic therapy and safety-net instructions.

Key Takeaways:
• Start prescribed stronger NSAID and may add paracetamol; always take with food.  
• Seek urgent care if pain escalates, new neurological symptoms appear, or vision changes worsen.  
• Book and attend in-person appointment for full examination and possible contraceptive review.

Next Steps:
• Schedule clinic visit for neurologic exam, funduscopy, and BP check.  
• Reassess headache pattern and response to medication; consider migraine prophylaxis or OCP change if migraine with aura confirmed.  
• Monitor and document any new or worsening symptoms; update care plan accordingly.

• Missing elements: Vital signs, objective neurologic and funduscopic findings, full medication list with dosages, past surgical history, complete family history (e.g., cardiovascular, cerebrovascular).  
• Internal conflicts: None noted.
